usage: native noun made from the verb 설레다 + the nominalizing -ㅁ, like 슬프다→슬픔; the sweet nervous buzz before something good
설렘 가득(한) drops the particle for a snappy, ad-like feel: 설렘 가득한 첫날
to feel one's heart pound with anticipation
the verb almost always travels with the mimetic 두근두근 (heart-thump)
the excitement of a first day at work
N + 의 + 설렘 names what the flutter is about; 여행의 설렘, 첫사랑의 설렘
examples: 내일 소풍이라 설렘 가득이에요.
Tomorrow's the picnic, so I'm full of excitement.
Simple A-is-B frame: 설렘 가득이에요 packages the whole feeling into one noun phrase.
첫 데이트 전날이라 설렘 때문에 잠이 안 와요.
It's the night before my first date, so I can't sleep from the butterflies.
설렘 때문에 = 'because of the flutter'; 때문에 attaches the cause to the noun, not a verb.
새집으로 이사 가는 날, 설렘 반 걱정 반이었어요.
On moving day to the new place, I was half excited and half anxious.
설렘 반 걱정 반 = the set 'half X, half Y' rhythm Koreans use for mixed feelings.
nuance: 설렘 is a warm, *positive* nervousness, the soft flutter before a date, a trip, or a new beginning, never fear or dread. It is native Korean (verb 설레다 + nominalizer -ㅁ, so spelled 설렘, not 설레임, the famous brand-name misspelling). The dividing line vs 신남/신나다 is anticipation vs the thing itself: 설렘 is the sweet buzzing *before* something, while 신나다 is the loud fun *during* it (a game, a party). It pairs constantly with the mimetic 두근두근 and the frame 설렘 반 걱정 반. The English-speaker trap is twofold: writing 설레임 (wrong) instead of 설렘, and conjugating the verb as 설레여요 when the correct present is 설레요 (stem 설레- + -어요 fuses to -레요).

usage: 여유 attaches to a domain word: 시간 여유, 돈 여유, 마음의 여유
to have no leeway / be stretched thin
the go-to soft refusal: covers money, time, OR emotional bandwidth
peace of mind / mental breathing room
literally 'leeway of the heart'; the most quoted collocation
the adjective made from 여유; 여유 자체 is a noun, not 여유하다
examples: 오늘은 시간 여유가 좀 있어요.
I have a little time to spare today.
Simple existence frame 여유가 있다/없다; here 여유 just means slack in the schedule.
주말엔 여유 있게 천천히 쉬고 싶어요.
On weekends I want to rest slowly, with some breathing room.
여유 있게 = 'in an unhurried way'; the adverbial -게 turns the state into how you do something.
월급 받아서 통장에 좀 여유가 생기면 여행 가려고요.
Once payday gives my account some room to breathe, I plan to travel.
여유가 생기다 = 'leeway comes into being'; 생기다 is the natural verb for slack appearing.
nuance: 여유 is one of the most useful daily nouns precisely because it stretches across three domains at once: spare *time*, spare *money*, and emotional *composure*. It is Sino-Korean 餘裕 (餘 'surplus/remainder' + 裕 'abundance'), literally 'left-over abundance', so picture margin or slack rather than emptiness. Koreans prize 마음의 여유 (room in the heart), so 여유가 없어요 is a gentle, relatable way to decline plans or admit stress without oversharing. The contrast to watch is 여유 (a noun = the slack itself) vs 여유롭다 (the adjective = being in a relaxed state); the English-speaker trap is inventing 여유하다, which does not exist. Use 여유가 있다/없다/생기다 for the noun, and 여유롭다 or 여유 있게 when you want the relaxed quality.

Limiting it to feelings only. 여유 equally covers 시간 여유 (spare time) and 돈 여유 (spare money), so 여유가 없어요 can mean broke, busy, OR frazzled depending on context.

usage: the verb; 후회 itself is the noun, so for the action use 후회하다
the feeling wells up on its own; slightly passive, less self-blaming than 후회하다
the motto phrase: 후회 없이 살자, 후회 없이 도전하다
set idiom (lit. 'beat the ground and regret') for deep, too-late regret
examples: 지금 안 사면 나중에 후회할 것 같아요.
If I don't buy it now, I think I'll regret it later.
Simple future hunch: 후회하다 + -ㄹ 것 같다 = 'I think I'll regret'; points forward to a choice not yet made.
그때 그 집 계약 안 한 게 두고두고 후회예요.
I keep regretting not signing the lease on that place back then.
Noun-as-predicate 후회예요; 두고두고 = 'over and over, lingeringly,' a perfect partner for regret.
후회 없이 도전해 보고 싶어요.
I want to give it a real try, with no regrets.
후회 없이 = the regret-free mindset phrase young Koreans love as a life motto.
nuance: 후회 is regret aimed squarely *backward* at a choice you already made, with a sting of self-blame. It is Sino-Korean 後悔 (後 'after/behind' + 悔 'to repent'), literally 'after-regret', the regret that comes *after* the deed. The verb 후회하다 is everyday, but the noun surfaces in lines like 후회예요 or 후회가 남아요, and the motto 후회 없이 (without regret) is hugely popular among 20-30s. The key synonym contrast is 후회 vs 아쉬움: 후회 blames *your own* decision ('I shouldn't have done that'), while 아쉬움 is a softer, fate-tinged 'aw, what a shame it didn't work out' with little self-blame. The English-speaker trap is mapping 'I regret it' straight to 후회해요 when you actually want the noun-predicate 후회예요 ('it's a regret'), and reaching for 후회 when the gentle 아쉬움 is what the situation calls for.

usage: the core collocation for both money and expectations: 월세가 부담이 돼요
adjective; the key word for politely declining an overly generous gesture
ultra-common host phrase that puts a guest at ease
pairs with its mirror 부담을 느끼다 (to feel the pressure)
examples: 월세가 좀 부담이 돼요.
The monthly rent is a bit of a burden.
Simple 부담이 되다 with money; here 부담 is plainly financial weight.
부담 갖지 말고 편하게 오세요.
Don't feel any pressure, just come and relax.
부담 갖지 말고 = the set host phrase; 갖지 말다 = 'don't hold (it).'
이렇게 비싼 선물은 부담스러워서 못 받겠어요.
A gift this expensive feels like too much, so I really can't accept it.
부담스럽다 in real social give-and-take = graceful refusal, not rudeness.
nuance: 부담 is essential for navigating Korean social give-and-take, where accepting too much puts you in someone's debt. It is Sino-Korean 負擔 (負 'to carry on the back' + 擔 'to shoulder'), literally 'a load you shoulder', and it covers both a *financial* weight (rent, a pricey gift) and an *emotional* one (expectations, obligation). When a host says 부담 갖지 마세요, they are pre-emptively lifting that load off you; when you call a gesture 부담스러워요, you are politely signaling 'this is too generous, I'd feel indebted.' The contrast to learn is 부담 (mental/social pressure or weight) vs 짐 (a literal piece of luggage, or a metaphorical 'I'm a burden to you' = 짐이 되다). The English-speaker trap is translating it only as 'burden' and missing the warm 'please don't trouble yourself' social move, and confusing the formal verb 부담하다 (to bear a *cost*, as in 비용을 부담하다) with feeling pressure, for which you want 부담스럽다 or 부담이 되다.

Saying 부담이 많다 for heavy pressure. The natural verb is 부담이 되다 or 부담이 크다, not 많다.

usage: verb form; 상대를 배려하다 = to consider the other person's situation
배려 + 心 = the trait; 배려심이 깊다 = deeply considerate
lit. 'consideration seat'; you'll literally read this on subway seats for the elderly/pregnant
graceful thank-you for someone easing your situation
examples: 배려해 주셔서 감사합니다.
Thank you for being so considerate.
Simple gratitude with 배려하다 + 주다 (do-for-me); the -아/어 주다 marks the kindness was for your benefit.
임산부 배려석은 비워 두는 게 좋아요.
It's best to keep the priority seats free for pregnant passengers.
배려석 = a real word on Seoul subways; 비워 두다 = 'leave it emptied.'
그 친구는 배려심이 깊어서 모두가 편하게 느껴요.
That friend is so deeply considerate that everyone feels at ease around them.
배려심이 깊다 = the fixed praise; 깊다 ('deep'), not 많다, is the natural partner.
nuance: 배려 is consideration shown through *action*, anticipating someone's needs and quietly easing their discomfort before they have to ask. It is Sino-Korean 配慮 (配 'to arrange/allot' + 慮 'to think over'), literally 'arranging your thinking around others', and it is one of the most praised qualities in Korea, so visible that subway seats are labeled 배려석 (consideration seats). The synonym contrast is 배려 vs 친절(親切): 친절 is surface-level *niceness/kindness* in the moment (a friendly clerk), while 배려 is the deeper, proactive reading of someone's situation and adjusting for it. The English-speaker trap is treating it as plain 'being nice' (that's 친절) and mixing up 배려 (an act / the behavior) with 배려심 (the inner *trait*): you thank someone for their 배려, but you describe a person as 배려심이 깊다.

Saying 배려가 많다 about a person. For the trait prefer 배려심이 깊다/많다; 배려 alone refers to the considerate act itself.

usage: THE collocation; the verb is 상하다 (to be spoiled/hurt), never 아프다
to have strong pride / be hard-headed about ego
세다 'strong' describes a prideful, won't-back-down person
to be stubborn out of pride
negative: refusing to bend just to save face
lit. 'bend one's pride,' as in apologizing first
examples: 그 말에 자존심이 좀 상했어요.
That remark hurt my pride a little.
Core frame 자존심이 상하다; note 상하다, the same verb used for food going bad — your pride 'spoils.'
걔는 자존심이 세서 먼저 연락 안 해요.
They've got such strong pride that they never reach out first.
자존심이 세다 paints a stubborn, face-saving personality; 세다 = 'strong/tough.'
사과하기 싫어서 자존심 부리다가 친구랑 멀어졌어요.
I let my stubborn pride win instead of apologizing, and drifted from my friend.
자존심 부리다 = acting out of ego; -다가 marks the action that led to a bad turn.
nuance: 자존심 is pride in the sense of the *ego you defend in front of others* — easily wounded, sometimes a flaw. It is Sino-Korean 自尊心 (自 'self' + 尊 'to honor' + 心 'heart'), literally 'self-honoring heart,' but in real use it leans outward and competitive. The crucial synonym contrast is 자존심 vs 자존감(自尊感): 자존심 looks *outward* (how others see you; it gets 상하다 'hurt' and you can 부리다 'wield' it stubbornly), whereas 자존감 is healthy *inner* self-worth that doesn't depend on winning face. This pair comes up constantly in relationship talk among 20-30s ('너 자존심 때문에 그래 vs 자존감을 키워'). The English-speaker trap is mapping the single English word 'pride' onto both, and choosing the wrong verb: pride does not 아프다 (ache) — it 상하다 (spoils/gets hurt).

Saying 자존심이 아프다. The fixed verb is 자존심이 상하다 (or 자존심을 다치다). 아프다 is for physical aches, not wounded pride.
Using 자존심 for proud-of-an-achievement pride. That positive 'I'm proud of you' is 자랑스럽다, a different word entirely.

usage: 생기다 = 'comes into being'; the natural verb for confidence forming after a small win
떨어지다 'to drop'; the mirror of 생기다
adverbial 있게 = the manner; 자신감 있게 발표하다 = present with confidence
examples: 면접을 잘 봐서 자신감이 생겼어요.
The interview went well, so I gained confidence.
Simple cause→effect with 자신감이 생기다; 면접을 보다 = 'to sit/take an interview.'
한국어로 말할 때 아직 자신감이 좀 부족해요.
I still lack a bit of confidence when speaking Korean.
자신감이 부족하다 = 'confidence is insufficient,' the everyday way to admit you feel unsure.
자신감 있게 발표했더니 칭찬을 받았어요.
I presented with confidence, and as a result I got praised.
자신감 있게 = the adverbial phrase; -았더니 reports the result of doing so.
nuance: 자신감 is confidence in *what you can do* — a skill, a task, a performance — and it is the everyday word for it. It is Sino-Korean 自信感 (自 'self' + 信 'to trust/believe' + 感 'feeling'), literally 'the feeling of trusting oneself.' Watch the close pair 자신 vs 자신감: 자신 (自信) is used predicatively as 자신 있어요 ('I'm sure I can do it') about a specific challenge, while 자신감 is the noun naming confidence as a *standing quality* (자신감이 있다/없다/생기다). The other contrast is 자신감 vs 자만심(自慢心): 자만심 is *over*confidence/conceit, the bad kind. The English-speaker trap is two-fold: inventing the verb 자신감하다 (impossible — it's a noun, so pair it with 있다/없다/생기다/넘치다), and over-claiming with 자신감 where a modest Korean would soften to 자신감이 좀 부족해요.

usage: to have a strong sense of responsibility
강하다 'strong' is the fixed partner; a top compliment at work
the plain existence form; 책임감이 없다 = irresponsible
adverbial; 책임감 있게 일하다 = to work responsibly
to take responsibility / take the blame
the verb (책임 + 지다 'to bear'); the action, not the feeling
examples: 그 사람은 책임감이 강해요.
That person has a strong sense of responsibility.
Simple trait statement; 책임감이 강하다 is the stock phrase, far more natural than 책임감이 많다.
반려동물을 키우려면 책임감이 꼭 필요해요.
If you're going to raise a pet, a sense of responsibility is essential.
책임감이 필요하다 = 'responsibility is needed'; -으려면 = 'if you intend to.'
맡은 일은 책임감 있게 끝까지 해낼게요.
I'll see the work I was given through to the end, responsibly.
책임감 있게 = adverbial; this is the line interviewers love to hear.
nuance: 책임감 is the *inner trait* of taking your duties seriously and owning the outcome, one of the most prized qualities in Korean workplaces. It is Sino-Korean 責任感 (責 'to hold accountable' + 任 'duty/charge' + 感 'feeling'), literally 'the feeling of accountability for one's duty,' so 책임감이 강하다 is a go-to compliment in references, interviews, and self-introductions. The contrast to nail is the 책임 family: 책임 (責任) is the *responsibility/duty itself* (책임을 지다 = to bear the responsibility), 책임감 is the *felt sense* of it (a character trait), and the verb 책임지다 means to *take the blame/charge* for a result. The English-speaker trap is collapsing all three into 'responsibility' and inventing 책임감하다 (impossible): pair the noun 책임감 with 있다/강하다, and switch to the verb 책임지다 when you mean the action of owning up.

Using 책임감하다. It is a noun — pair it with 있다/강하다/없다. For the verb 'take responsibility,' use 책임지다.
Saying 책임감이 많다. The idiomatic verb is 책임감이 강하다 (strong), not 많다 (many).

usage: 강하다/많다 are the natural partners for the trait
the situation-needs-it frame: 공부엔 인내심이 필요해요
vivid: 바닥나다 'to hit bottom,' patience all used up
가지고 = 'holding,' i.e. patiently keep at it
examples: 한국어 공부는 인내심이 정말 필요해요.
Studying Korean really takes patience.
Simple 인내심이 필요하다 (patience is needed); great for talking about long-haul learning.
아이들을 가르치려면 인내심이 많아야 해요.
To teach kids, you need a lot of patience.
인내심이 많다 + -아야 하다 ('must have'); -으려면 sets up the goal.
줄이 너무 길어서 인내심이 바닥났어요.
The line was so long that I ran clean out of patience.
인내심이 바닥나다 = the colorful 'patience hit rock bottom,' perfect for venting.
nuance: 인내심 is patience as the *strength to endure* hardship and long waits, a character trait, somewhat more formal and dignified than the everyday verb 참다 (to put up with / hold it in). It is Sino-Korean 忍耐心 (忍 'to endure' + 耐 'to withstand' + 心 'heart'), literally 'an enduring heart.' You describe people with 인내심이 강하다/많다 and confess 인내심이 바닥났어요 when you've had it. The synonym contrast is 인내심 (the standing capacity to endure, a noun) vs 참다 (the moment-to-moment act of bearing something: 화를 참다 = to hold back anger). The English-speaker trap is two-fold: inventing 인내심하다 (it's a noun — use 인내심이 있다/많다 or the verbs 참다/견디다), and over-reaching for this somewhat lofty word in casual griping where the plain 참았어요 ('I put up with it') sounds far more natural.

Saying 인내심이 세다. Unlike 자존심이 세다, patience takes 강하다/많다, not 세다.

usage: 생기다/들다 are the verbs; N에 호기심이 생기다 = curious about N
warm compliment about an eager, open personality
out of curiosity / on a whim
handy reason-marker: 호기심에 한번 해 봤어요
자극하다 'to stimulate'; ads and teasers 호기심을 자극하다
examples: 저는 호기심이 많아요.
I'm a very curious person.
Simple trait line; 호기심이 많다 is the set phrase, a gentle compliment if said of others.
새로 생긴 카페에 호기심이 생겨서 가 봤어요.
I got curious about the newly-opened cafe, so I went and checked it out.
N에 호기심이 생기다 — the target of curiosity takes 에, not 을/를.
호기심에 한국 예능을 봤다가 푹 빠졌어요.
Out of curiosity I watched a Korean variety show, and ended up totally hooked.
호기심에 = 'on a whim'; -다가 marks the shift from a casual try to getting absorbed.
nuance: 호기심 is curiosity, the itch to *find out* or *try* something new, and 호기심이 많다 is a warm compliment about an open, eager mind. It is Sino-Korean 好奇心 (好 'to like/be fond of' + 奇 'novel/strange' + 心 'heart'), literally 'a heart fond of the novel.' The super-handy adverbial 호기심에 ('out of curiosity, on a whim') explains why you impulsively tried something. The key synonym contrast is 호기심 vs 관심(關心): 호기심 is the short, sparky urge to *know what something is* (a new shop, a weird headline), while 관심 is sustained *interest or care* you keep over time (관심 분야 = field of interest; 관심 있어요 about a person you fancy). The English-speaker trap is choosing 호기심 for a lasting interest (use 관심), and inventing 호기심하다 — the noun pairs with 생기다/들다/많다, and crucially its target takes the particle 에 (…에 호기심이 생기다), not 을/를.

usage: 들다 'to arise' is the standard everyday partner
느끼다; a touch more formal/deliberate than 들다
시달리다 'to be harassed by'; for heavy, lingering guilt
남다 'to remain'; the guilt that stays with you afterward
examples: 야식을 먹어서 죄책감이 들어요.
I ate a late-night snack, so I feel guilty.
Light, everyday 죄책감이 들다 — Koreans use it even for diet slip-ups, not just serious wrongs.
바쁘다고 부모님께 자주 연락 못 해서 죄책감이 좀 있어요.
I feel a little guilty for not calling my parents often, using being busy as an excuse.
죄책감이 있다 = 'to carry guilt'; …다고 reports the excuse you're making.
그때 거짓말한 게 계속 죄책감으로 남았어요.
The lie I told back then stayed with me as guilt.
죄책감으로 남다 = the guilt that lingers; 거짓말한 게 = 'the fact that I lied' as the subject.
nuance: 죄책감 is the *inward* feeling of guilt over something you did wrong — the weight on your own conscience. It is Sino-Korean 罪責感 (罪 'sin/wrong' + 責 'blame/accountability' + 感 'feeling'), literally 'the feeling of being to blame for a wrong,' and it pairs most naturally with 들다 (죄책감이 들어요). Notice 20-30s use it *lightly* too — about late-night snacks or skipping the gym — not only grave offenses. The essential synonym contrast is 죄책감 vs 미안함: 죄책감 is the *internal* guilt toward yourself/your conscience, while 미안함 is the feeling of being *sorry toward another person* (and 미안하다 is what you actually say to them). The English-speaker trap is inventing 죄책감하다 (it's a noun — use 들다/느끼다), and using 죄책감 where you really mean apologizing to someone, which calls for 미안하다/미안함.

usage: the standard collocation; 느끼다 'to feel' is the natural verb
보람이 있다/없다 judges whether effort paid off
the adjective from 보람; 보람찬 하루 = a fulfilling day
describes a job that gives a sense of meaning
examples: 오늘 할 일을 다 끝내서 보람이 있었어요.
I finished everything I had to do today, so it felt worthwhile.
Simple 보람이 있다 = 'there was a sense of reward'; the payoff of a productive day.
힘들었지만 일을 마치고 나니 보람을 느꼈어요.
It was hard, but once I wrapped up the work, I felt a real sense of fulfillment.
보람을 느끼다 after effort; -고 나니 = 'after doing, I found that…'
가르치던 학생이 시험에 합격해서 정말 보람찬 하루였어요.
A student I'd been teaching passed the exam, so it was a truly fulfilling day.
보람차다 → 보람찬 (modifier form) + 하루; the fixed phrase 보람찬 하루.
nuance: 보람 is the warm payoff feeling when your effort proves *worthwhile* — the quiet reward of seeing hard work bear fruit. It is a *native* Korean word (no hanja), which is part of why it has no clean one-word English equivalent; 'fulfillment / sense of reward / worthwhileness' all circle it. Koreans use it about jobs, study, volunteering, and parenting: 보람을 느끼다 (to feel fulfilled), 보람이 있다 (it was worth it), and the adjective 보람차다 (보람찬 하루 = a fulfilling day). The synonym contrast is 보람 vs 만족(滿足): 만족 is general *satisfaction* with any outcome (a good meal, a fair price), while 보람 specifically requires that your *effort/contribution* made it meaningful — you earned it. The English-speaker trap is reducing it to a material 'reward' (a prize or money is 상/보상, not 보람), and inventing 보람하다 — use 보람을 느끼다, 보람이 있다, or the adjective 보람차다.
